claims.text: The onset of premelting in HEA nanoparticles is primarily governed by the degree of surface chemical ordering or elemental segregation.
The overall melting behavior of HEA nanoparticles is primarily governed by the degree of surface chemical ordering or elemental segregation.
Uniform surface mixing strengthens surface bonding relative to a segregated, compositionally heterogeneous surface.
Uniform surface mixing delays premelting relative to surface segregation.
Rapid-quench synthesis typically produces HEA nanoparticles with some surface elemental segregation.
Post-synthesis thermal annealing promotes atomic mixing and reduces surface compositional heterogeneity.
Segregated surface regions have locally lower cohesive energy.
Low-cohesive-energy surface regions act as nucleation sites for premelting.
Annealing-induced surface homogenization produces more uniformly high bond strengths.
More uniformly high surface bond strengths raise the activation barrier for surface-atom mobility.
A higher activation barrier for surface-atom mobility delays the onset of premelting.
Annealed, homogenized nanoparticles will exhibit a later onset of surface premelting than as-cast, segregated nanoparticles of the same nominal composition and size distribution.
Annealed, homogenized nanoparticles will exhibit a higher overall melting temperature than the as-cast baseline.
The predicted effects will be consistent for nanoparticles between 5 and 20 nm in diameter.
The proposed relationship applies to HEAs containing at least five principal elements with moderate atomic-size mismatches.
Surface effects dominate the thermal behavior of HEA nanoparticles in the stated 5–20 nm size range.
The magnitudes of premelting and melting-temperature changes may depend on elemental combination, synthesis reproducibility, and particle size.
Strain and defect density may independently influence premelting and melting behavior.
